explanation: Wigner's 1939 idea for classifying particles: fix the particle's momentum, then ask which spacetime symmetries leave it alone. Those leftover transformations, the little group, are what can still act on the particle's internal state, so they determine its spin. For a massive particle you can stand in its rest frame; the momentum (m, 0, 0, 0) is untouched by every spatial rotation, so the little group is the rotation group (SU(2) at the spinor level), and spin is quantized in the familiar way. Massless particles get a different little group and carry only a helicity. In this project, splitting a massive momentum into two null spinors is not unique: the leftover freedom is a U(2), which factors into the massive little group SU(2) (the spin frame) and a phase circle used as a clock.
why: Little groups are the backbone of the particle concept: Wigner's classification says a particle is an irreducible representation labeled by mass and its little-group spin. In this project, recovering SU(2) inside the minimal-split U(2) is evidence the null-split formalism carries genuine spin, plus an extra determinant-line phase interpreted as a proper-time clock.
example: For momentum (m, 0, 0, 0) every rotation about any axis leaves it fixed, so the little group is SU(2); for a light-like momentum along z, rotations about z survive but boosts along z rescale the null vector.
conventions: Whether one works with SO(3) or its double cover SU(2) (spinor conventions), and whether the split freedom is quoted as U(2) or SU(2) x U(1), are labeling choices; the project uses the spinor-level split U(2) = spin x clock and tags the SU(2) little-group identification as an import in the P1 manuscript.
source_refs: Wigner 1939 On unitary representations of the inhomogeneous Lorentz group

summary: The Lorentz group is the group of linear transformations of 4-dimensional spacetime that preserve the Minkowski metric eta (rotations plus boosts); in this project link transports and frame changes are required to be eta-Lorentz, realized concretely through SL(2,C).
explanation: Ordinary rotations are the transformations that keep lengths fixed. Special relativity replaces length with the spacetime interval, which combines time and space with opposite signs, and the Lorentz group is the set of all linear transformations that keep that interval fixed. It contains rotations of space plus boosts, which relate observers moving at constant velocity. Because you can compose two such transformations and undo any of them, they form a group. Spin-1/2 objects transform not under the Lorentz group itself but under its double cover, realized by SL(2,C), the 2x2 complex matrices of determinant 1; the two matrices +M and -M give the same Lorentz transformation. In this project every link transport and frame change is required to preserve eta in exactly this sense.
why: The Lorentz group is the symmetry backbone of special relativity and of every relativistic field theory. In this project recovering Lorentz behavior from finite null-edge data is a central goal, so the group appears both as a target (invariance claims are gated) and as a tool (eta-Lorentz transports and SL(2,C) actions inside kernel-checked statements).
example: A boost along the x-axis mixes t and x (like a rotation, but with hyperbolic functions) while leaving t^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 unchanged, so both observers measure the same speed of light.
conventions: The project metric signature is locked mostly-minus, (+,-,-,-), so eta-Lorentz means preserving that eta. SL(2,C) covers the Lorentz group two-to-one. Project results carefully distinguish proper eta-Lorentz transformations from proper-orthochronous ones; do not upgrade one to the other without proof.

summary: Lorentz invariance is the symmetry of special relativity: physics looks the same after rotations and boosts, with one light speed for all observers; this project withdraws exact Lorentz-invariance claims for finite-valency null graphs pending the L0 no-go gate.
explanation: Special relativity's core symmetry: no experiment run inside a sealed, uniformly moving lab can reveal the motion, and everyone measures the same speed of light. The transformations connecting moving observers, rotations plus boosts (which mix space and time), form the Lorentz group, and a Lorentz-invariant theory treats them all as symmetries. Discrete models have a problem: a lattice singles out preferred directions, and a boost stretches null directions by arbitrary factors, so a graph in which each event touches only finitely many null edges is expected to break exact boost symmetry. This project takes that seriously: exact claims for its finite-valency null graphs are withdrawn, Gate L0 aims to prove the no-go outright, and ontology statements use Poisson-sprinkled causal orders, which are Lorentz invariant in distribution; the tetrahedral lattice is a gauge-fixed regulator.
why: Lorentz invariance is among the most precisely tested facts in physics, so any discrete spacetime program must explain how it survives the continuum limit. In this project the bookkeeping of regulator versus ontology, and exact versus in-distribution symmetry, is a standing guardrail on every headline claim.
example: A boost with rapidity eta multiplies a right-moving null momentum by e^eta and a left-moving one by e^(-eta); any fixed finite set of null directions gets smeared apart, which is the intuition behind the L0 no-go target.
conventions: Metric signature must be declared per module (project physics-conventions rule). Claim hygiene: 'Lorentz invariant in distribution' (sprinkled causal sets) is distinct from exact invariance of a fixed graph, and NULL_EDGE_RESULTS keeps SL(2,C) invariance of the determinant mass in the draft tier pending semantic review.

summary: A mass gap is a strictly positive minimum energy separating a system's ground state from all its excitations, so nothing arbitrarily light can be created; in lattice audits a branch counts as removed only when the inverse propagator is gapped there.
explanation: Think of a system's possible energies as rungs on a ladder. The ground state is the floor, and the mass gap is the height of the first rung above the floor. If the gap is zero, arbitrarily gentle excitations exist, like long slow ripples on water; if it is positive, every excitation costs at least a fixed minimum energy, and the lightest particle has nonzero mass. In this project the idea appears in lattice audits: unwanted fermion branches (doublers and mirror modes) count as removed only if the inverse propagator is pushed away from zero on them by a quantified amount, such as the Wilson bound r W(q), not merely because the propagator itself happens to vanish somewhere.
why: Whether four-dimensional Yang-Mills theory has a mass gap is a Clay Millennium Prize problem, so the notion sits at the frontier of mathematical physics. In this project the ghost rule attributed to Golterman-Shamir makes a true inverse-propagator gap the mandatory standard for removing doubler and mirror branches in any chiral release audit.
example: On the lattice torus the scalar Wilson weight W(q) = sum_a (1 - cos q_a) vanishes only at q = 0, so the shifted symbol A(q) + r W(q) I is gapped by at least r W(q) at every non-origin momentum: doubler branches are removed by a genuine gap, without classifying the full zero locus.
conventions: Locked project rule: no gauge-charged branch may be removed solely by a propagator zero (Golterman-Shamir ghost rule); removal must come from a true inverse-propagator mass gap, quantified when possible, e.g. the Wilson bound r W(q) with W(q) >= 0.
notation: Delta = E_1 - E_0; Wilson bound r W(q)
source_refs: Jaffe and Witten, Clay Millennium Problem statement: Yang-Mills existence and mass gap

summary: The mass shell is the set of energy-momentum combinations allowed for a free particle of mass m, given by p^2 = m^2 in mostly-minus signature (equivalently E^2 = p^2 + m^2 with c = 1); physical particles are said to be on shell.
explanation: A free particle cannot have just any combination of energy and momentum: relativity ties them together by E^2 = (pc)^2 + (m c^2)^2. If you plot allowed energy against momentum, the allowed points form a curved surface, a hyperboloid, called the mass shell. Being 'on shell' means physically allowed; internal, virtual processes can be 'off shell'. Written with four-vectors in the project's mostly-minus sign convention, the condition is simply p^2 = m^2. In this project the spectral mass-shell matching theorem aims to show that the null-edge wave operator reproduces exactly this condition: solutions of -Box_null + Phi^2 = 0 should satisfy p^2 = m^2, and doubling checks must test det D(q) = 0 or this mass-shell condition, not weaker coefficient conditions.
why: The mass shell is the dividing line between real particles and virtual ones, and every dispersion relation is a statement about its shape. In this project it is the target of the spectral mass-shell matching theorem and the determinant-level standard that doubling tests must meet.
example: A photon (m = 0) lives on the light cone E = |p|; an electron lives on the hyperboloid E^2 = p^2 + m_e^2, whose lowest point E = m_e is the rest energy.
conventions: The project uses mostly-minus metric signature (+,-,-,-), so the on-shell condition reads p^2 = m^2. Box_null is the kinetic mass-shell operator with plane-wave symbol -p^2, and the normalization -Box_null + Phi^2 = 0 is fixed to reproduce p^2 = m^2. Doubling tests must be determinant-level: det D(q) = 0 or the corresponding mass-shell equation.

summary: The pattern of plus and minus signs in the spacetime distance formula; this project locks the mostly-minus choice +(time)^2 - (space)^2, under which null momenta satisfy p^2 = 0 and massive on-shell particles satisfy p^2 = m^2.
explanation: In ordinary geometry, the squared length of a vector adds the squares of all its components. Spacetime geometry modifies Pythagoras: the time component and the space components enter with opposite signs. The metric signature records which signs go where. With mostly-minus signature, a spacetime vector p has squared length p^2 = p_0^2 - p_1^2 - p_2^2 - p_3^2. A light ray's momentum has p^2 = 0, because the time and space parts exactly balance, while a massive particle at rest has p^2 = m^2 > 0. The opposite convention, mostly-plus, flips every sign, so massive particles get p^2 = -m^2 instead. Nothing physical changes between the two choices, but every formula's signs do, which is why a project must pick one signature and never silently mix them.
why: Half the sign errors in relativistic physics come from mixing signature conventions between sources. This repo's null-edge program is built on statements like p^2 = 0 for null edges, so the locked mostly-minus signature is load-bearing for nearly every mass and Dirac-square theorem.
example: For a photon moving along x with energy E, p = (E, E, 0, 0), so p^2 = E^2 - E^2 = 0: null. For an electron at rest, p = (m, 0, 0, 0), so p^2 = m^2.
conventions: Locked mostly-minus: +(time)^2 - (space)^2, i.e. (+,-,-,-). Null momenta obey p^2 = 0 and massive on-shell modes obey p^2 = m^2. Any theorem using the opposite signature must live behind an explicit namespace or conversion lemma (docs/CONVENTIONS.md, status Locked).

summary: A no-go theorem is a rigorous proof that a construction or scenario is impossible under stated assumptions, such as the Nielsen-Ninomiya ban on naive chiral lattice fermions; this project collects kernel-checked no-gos as guardrails for its program.
explanation: A no-go theorem does not just fail to find a construction; it proves that no construction of that kind can exist. Compare the classic puzzle of tiling a chessboard with two opposite corners removed using dominoes: a counting argument shows it is impossible, no matter how clever you are. Physics has famous examples, like the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem forbidding naive chiral fermions on a lattice. This project deliberately collects kernel-checked no-gos as guardrails: no polynomial filter can select physical states from one-sided retarded transport, a bare graph cannot canonically supply a tetrad, the scalar Wilson route to a chiral release is closed, and no estimator can recover an absolute length scale from scale-blind observations. Each no-go records exactly which assumptions it needs, which marks the surviving escape routes.
why: No-go theorems save research programs from dead ends by turning 'we could not find it' into 'it cannot exist'. In this project they are kernel-checked and treated as program assets: each one closes a route and precisely marks the escape hatches that remain open.
example: The project's retarded-filter no-go: any weighted strict-past operator on a finite causal order is scalar-plus-nilpotent, and such an operator admits no nonzero proper idempotent polynomial filter, so physical-state selection cannot come from one-sided retarded transport alone.
conventions: A no-go theorem forbids only what its hypotheses cover. The project convention is to state assumptions explicitly and record which routes remain open; for example, the retarded-filter no-go leaves symmetric pairings, constraint kernels, and richer probe representations available.
source_refs: Nielsen and Ninomiya 1981, lattice fermion doubling no-go theorem

summary: A null spinor is a two-component complex vector that acts as the square root of a lightlike momentum; in this project's draft program two null spinors span a complex area z whose modulus is the derived rest energy.
explanation: A lightlike (null) momentum, like a photon's, can be written as the 'square' of a simpler object: a two-component complex vector psi, with the momentum recovered as the matrix psi psi-dagger. That vector is a null spinor. Two null spinors psi and phi together build a massive momentum P_tot = psi psi-dagger + phi phi-dagger, and the interesting quantity is the complex area z = psi wedge phi, the parallelogram-like area the two spinors span. In this project's draft manuscript, the modulus |z| is the derived rest energy: mass appears as the area between two null directions. When the spinors become collinear the area vanishes and the gap closes, which is exactly the massless boundary of the construction.
why: Null spinors reduce statements about lightlike momenta to linear algebra in C^2 and underlie spinor-helicity and twistor methods used across particle physics. In this project they are the raw input of the area-to-mass construction: the program's central draft claim is that rest energy is the area spanned by two null spinors.
example: psi = (1,0) and phi = (0,1) give z = psi wedge phi = 1 and P_tot = the identity matrix, a unit rest energy at rest; choosing phi = 2 psi instead gives z = 0, the collinear massless boundary where the gap closes.
conventions: Spinors are two-component vectors in C^2 transforming under SL(2,C); the project metric is mostly-minus. A common overall phase of the spinor pair is a basis choice, so only the relative orientation of z is physical, and SL(2,C) covariance of the input map does not make the finite lattice dynamics exactly Lorentz invariant (a stated program boundary, not established physics).
notation: psi, phi in C^2; z = psi wedge phi; mu = |z|
source_refs: Penrose and Rindler, Spinors and Space-Time (two-spinor calculus)

summary: An overlap fermion is a lattice fermion whose Dirac operator is built from the sign function of a Hermitian kernel, evading the doubling problem while keeping an exact lattice chiral symmetry through the Ginsparg-Wilson relation, at the price of nonlocality.
explanation: Discretizing fermions on a lattice spawns unwanted extra copies called doublers. Wilson's fix removes them but destroys chiral symmetry, the independent treatment of left-handed and right-handed parts. Overlap fermions are a smarter fix: the Dirac operator is built from the sign function of a Hermitian kernel, and the result satisfies the Ginsparg-Wilson relation, which restores an exact lattice version of chiral symmetry. The price is nonlocality: every site talks to every other site, though with rapidly decaying strength. In this project the overlap construction is a fallback escape route from doubling, with an explicit caution flag: applying the unprojected overlap directly to the bare operator D_+ is labeled unsafe, because an unwanted branch crossing the shifted kernel's mass shell would make the sign function singular.
why: Overlap fermions showed that exact chiral symmetry on the lattice is possible, resolving a decades-old tension with the doubling no-go theorems. In this project they are a fallback escape route for the chiral release gates, admissible only under an explicit safety condition on the bare operator.
example: Neuberger's construction takes the Wilson Dirac operator with a negative mass shift, forms the Hermitian kernel H = gamma5 D_W, and defines the fermion from Dov = 1 + gamma5 sign(H); doublers are removed while an exact lattice chiral symmetry survives.
conventions: Project safety convention: direct unprojected overlap on the full bare D_+ is labeled unsafe until a shifted-kernel branch analysis is done. The sanctioned routes are a genuine branch classifier or projector first, or a controlled domain-wall or projected-overlap construction after the branch split.
source_refs: Neuberger 1998, overlap Dirac operator

summary: The overlap operator Dov = 1 + gamma5 sign(H) is a lattice Dirac operator built from the matrix sign function of a gapped Hermitian kernel H; it satisfies the Ginsparg-Wilson relation exactly and carries an integer chiral index.
explanation: Take a Hermitian matrix H with no zero eigenvalues; for lattice fermions H is typically gamma5 times a Wilson Dirac operator with a negative mass shift. Its sign function sign(H) keeps each eigenvector but replaces the eigenvalue by +1 or -1. The overlap operator is then Dov = 1 + gamma5 sign(H). This simple recipe has remarkable consequences: Dov satisfies the Ginsparg-Wilson relation exactly, and it carries an integer chiral index counting protected zero modes. In this project the index calculus is machine-checked: the index is an integer, equals half a signature difference, is invariant under unitary conjugation and under the choice of certified sign, and an invertible Dov forces index zero, so a nonzero index forces an exact zero mode. These results drive the C2 gauge gates.
why: The overlap operator is the cleanest known bridge between lattice regularization and chiral topology: its integer index is a finite, computable stand-in for the continuum anomaly story. In this project that index calculus is kernel-checked in draft modules and drives the C2 gauge gates, including the vanishing theorem tying a nonzero index to exact zero modes.
example: In the project's kernel-checked flux witness, threading a gauge flux through one plaquette of a small hopping model yields overlap index -1 while the zero-flux model has index 0; by the vanishing theorem the flux model must therefore host an exact zero mode.
conventions: Project normalization: Dov = 1 + gamma5 sign(H), with the Ginsparg-Wilson relation written gamma5 D + D gamma5 = D gamma5 D and index densities using f (1 - (1/2) Dov). The certified-sign interface pins sign(H) uniquely through positive-semidefinite square-root uniqueness, avoiding functional calculus and eigendecompositions.
source_refs: Neuberger 1998, overlap Dirac operator
Ginsparg and Wilson 1982, remnant chiral symmetry on the lattice

summary: Parallel transport is the rule for carrying a vector or internal state along a path so it stays as constant as the geometry allows, implemented on graphs by an invertible map on each directed edge; transporting around loops detects curvature.
explanation: Carry an arrow along a path on a curved surface, keeping it as straight as the surface allows. On a sphere, going around a triangle brings the arrow back rotated: transport around loops detects curvature. Abstractly, parallel transport assigns to every step of a path an invertible map; for gauge fields on a graph, that is a matrix on each directed edge saying how data at one end is expressed at the other. In this project the finite carrier operator is assembled from null directions, transports, a chirality grading, and a turn amplitude, and a machine-checked draft theorem says the chiral index is invariant under every choice of potential and transport: transports can move mass around, but they can never change the number of protected massless modes.
why: Parallel transport is the common language of general relativity (moving vectors through curved spacetime) and gauge theory (moving charged states through a field). In this project it fills a named slot in the carrier operator, and the transport-independence of the chiral index is the program's machine-checked statement that masslessness protection is topological.
example: Carry an arrow from the north pole down to the equator, a quarter of the way around the equator, and back up: it returns rotated by 90 degrees even though it was never twisted; the rotation equals the enclosed spherical area. On a lattice the same bookkeeping is one matrix per directed edge.
conventions: Transports live on directed links, and reversing a link inverts the map; curvature lives in loops around oriented faces. The project's transported finite-fiber control uses a Euclidean transpose pairing that must not be identified with Lorentz transport by notation alone; the Krein bridge uses A^sharp = J A^T J with J = diag(+,+,+,-,-,-) derived from the mostly-minus metric.
notation: U(e) on each directed edge e

summary: One of three 2x2 complex matrices sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 that are Hermitian, square to the identity, and anticommute pairwise; they describe spin-1/2, and in this project they solder four-momenta to 2x2 Hermitian matrices and realize the derived weak-isospin action.
explanation: The three Pauli matrices are the simplest nontrivial quantum operators: sigma_1 = [[0,1],[1,0]], sigma_2 = [[0,-i],[i,0]], sigma_3 = [[1,0],[0,-1]]. Each is Hermitian (equal to its own conjugate transpose), each squares to the identity, and any two distinct ones anticommute. Think of them as the three independent ways to flip or phase a two-state system, like a coin that can also pick up complex phases. Together with the identity matrix they form a basis for all 2x2 Hermitian matrices, which is why a four-momentum p can be packaged as the single matrix p_0 I + p . sigma. In this project that packaging, called soldering, turns null momenta into rank-one matrices, and the Dixon weak-isospin operators act as literal Pauli matrices on a two-dimensional mode plane.
why: Pauli matrices are the smallest Clifford algebra and the building blocks of gamma matrices, spinors, and qubit operations. In this repo they carry two loads: the momentum soldering p_0 I + p . sigma behind the Plucker-mass theorems, and the tau-hat weak-isospin action derived in the Dixon algebra work.
example: sigma_1 swaps the two basis states, a pure bit flip: sigma_1 (a, b) = (b, a). Check anticommutation: sigma_1 sigma_2 = i sigma_3 while sigma_2 sigma_1 = -i sigma_3, so sigma_1 sigma_2 + sigma_2 sigma_1 = 0.
conventions: Standard basis with sigma_3 diagonal, diag(1,-1). Soldering convention: p becomes p_0 I + p . sigma in mostly-minus signature, so det(p_0 I + p . sigma) = p^2. In the Dixon weak-isospin work the tau-hat operators act on the (v, nu) mode basis as sigma_1, sigma_2, and minus sigma_3; the sign on sigma_3 is part of the recorded convention (Sources/Dixon_CxHxO_Convention_Reference.md).
notation: sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 (also sigma_x, sigma_y, sigma_z); p . sigma

summary: A plaquette is an elementary oriented face of a lattice or graph, the smallest closed loop of edges; multiplying edge transport matrices around it gives a holonomy whose deviation from the identity measures the local field strength or curvature.
explanation: Picture a wire fence: the wires are edges of a lattice, and each smallest rectangle of wires is a plaquette, an elementary face with a chosen direction of travel around its boundary. In lattice gauge theory each edge carries a transport matrix; multiplying the matrices around a plaquette gives the plaquette holonomy, and how far it sits from the identity measures the field strength, or curvature, threading that little face. In this project the division of labor is explicit: gravitational transport lives on directed links, while finite curvature lives in plaquette holonomy on oriented faces, which transforms covariantly under vertex gauge changes. Plaquettes also matter for fermions here: threading gauge flux through a single plaquette shifts the overlap chiral index.
why: Plaquettes are where local field strength becomes computable on a lattice: Wilson built quantum gauge theory from a sum over plaquettes. In this project they carry the curvature half of the transport-versus-curvature split and supply the flux witnesses that shift the overlap chiral index in the C2 gates.
example: In a square lattice gauge theory the plaquette variable U_p = U1 U2 U3^-1 U4^-1 multiplies the four edge matrices around one face; for weak fields the quantity 1 - Re tr U_p is proportional to the squared field strength through the face, which is why Wilson's action sums it over all plaquettes.
conventions: Orientation matters: reversing the traversal direction inverts the plaquette holonomy. Project split: gravitational transport lives on directed links and curvature on oriented faces; plaquette holonomy is conjugation-covariant under vertex gauge changes, and coframe-pair labels must be kept distinct from curvature-face labels.
source_refs: Wilson 1974, Confinement of quarks (lattice gauge theory)

summary: A propagator is a field's response function, describing how a disturbance at one point is felt at another; its momentum-space poles, where the inverse propagator vanishes, mark physical particles and their masses.
explanation: Drop a pebble in a pond: the spreading ripple pattern is the pond's response to a poke at one point. A propagator is the field-theory version; it records how a disturbance created at one point is felt at another. In momentum space a typical propagator looks like 1/(p^2 - m^2): it blows up (has a pole) exactly on the mass shell, which is how particles and masses show up in calculations. The inverse propagator is often the more honest object: particles live where it vanishes, and an unwanted mode is truly gone only where the inverse propagator stays a bounded distance from zero. In this project release audits require exactly that, a true inverse-propagator mass gap, because a mere propagator zero can hide a ghost that still couples to gauge fields.
why: Almost every quantity in quantum field theory is computed by stitching propagators together, and particle masses are read off from where the inverse propagator vanishes. In this project the distinction between a propagator zero and an inverse-propagator gap is a locked audit rule for any claimed removal of unwanted branches.
example: A free scalar field has momentum-space propagator 1/(p^2 - m^2), with the pole at p^2 = m^2 being the particle. An unwanted branch whose propagator merely vanishes at a point is not truly gone: once gauge fields couple to it, it can return as a ghost, so genuine removal requires the inverse propagator to be gapped on that branch.
conventions: Locked project rule: no gauge-charged branch may be removed solely by a propagator zero; a release audit must exhibit a true inverse-propagator mass gap on mirror or unwanted branches, plus ghost-zero safety and positive physical residues. The project's mostly-minus signature puts the pole at p^2 = m^2.

summary: Proper time is the time read by a clock carried along a particle's own path through spacetime, an observer-independent quantity that vanishes along light rays; in this project 'proper time = det-line holonomy / 2m' is a labeled postulate, not a theorem.
explanation: Strap a watch to a particle: proper time is what that watch reads along the particle's path through spacetime, and all observers agree on it. A traveling twin ages by proper time, which can be less than the stay-at-home twin's coordinate time. Along a path it accumulates as d tau^2 = dt^2 - dx^2 (with c = 1), so light itself accumulates none: null paths have zero proper time. In this project a massive particle's internal clock is modeled by the determinant line of its minimal null split, which rotates at angular frequency 2m under free Dirac evolution. The identification 'proper time = det-line holonomy / 2m' is explicitly a labeled postulate of the program, not a theorem, and aggregate proper time arises only from endpoint geometry of null ticks.
why: Proper time is the physical time of relativity: particle lifetimes, aging, and clock readings all follow it rather than coordinate time. In this project it marks a carefully policed claim boundary: the det-line clock rotating at frequency 2m is a theorem, but calling that rotation proper time is a labeled postulate under the program's claim discipline.
example: Muons created high in the atmosphere decay after about 2.2 microseconds of proper time, yet many reach the ground: at near-light speed their proper time accumulates far more slowly than ground coordinate time, so from our viewpoint their internal clocks run slow.
conventions: Mostly-minus signature and c = 1, so d tau^2 = dt^2 - dx^2 along a worldline. Claim discipline: 'proper time = det-line holonomy / 2m' is a labeled postulate, not a theorem; the kernel-checked aggregate identity concerns endpoint Lorentzian geometry, not positive proper time on individual null edges.

summary: A quantum cellular automaton (QCA) is a rule that updates quantum data on a lattice in discrete time steps, acting unitarily (probability preserving and reversible) and strictly locally, so influence can spread at most a fixed number of cells per step.
explanation: Picture a huge grid of cells, each holding a small quantum state. At every tick of a clock one fixed rule updates the whole grid at once, mixing each cell only with its near neighbors. Two properties make this a quantum cellular automaton: the update is unitary, meaning total probability is exactly preserved and the step can be undone, and it is strictly local, meaning information can hop at most a fixed number of cells per tick, so influence stays inside a rigid cone. It is like Conway's Game of Life upgraded to quantum rules and made reversible. In this project the 3+1 dimensional walk underlying the null-edge program is kernel-checked to have exact norm preservation, a two-sided inverse, and a strict causal cone.
why: QCAs are the strictest discrete substitute for relativistic quantum fields: unitarity supplies quantum mechanics and the strict cone supplies a built-in speed limit. In this project the QCA properties of the 3+1 walk are the evidence that the null-edge dynamics is genuinely local and reversible, exactly and not just approximately.
example: A one-dimensional Dirac QCA alternates a shift step (left-movers move one cell left, right-movers one cell right) with a local mass coin that mixes the two components at each site; at small mass and long wavelength its behavior approaches the Dirac equation.
conventions: Locality here means a strict causal cone (exactly zero amplitude outside the cone after each step), not merely exponentially small tails; the project distinguishes this strict QCA property from approximate locality, and its causal-cone statements are proved at that strict level.
source_refs: Arrighi 2019 overview of quantum cellular automata

summary: Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is the established quantum field theory of the strong force, in which quarks carrying three kinds of color charge exchange gluons; it binds quarks into protons and neutrons and generates most visible mass as binding energy.
explanation: QCD describes the strongest of nature's forces. Quarks carry a three-valued charge whimsically called color, and they interact by exchanging gluons, which themselves carry color. Because the force carriers interact with each other, the force does not fade with distance, so quarks can never be pulled free: they stay confined inside composite particles such as protons and neutrons. Almost all of a proton's mass is the trapped energy of this quark-gluon system, not the tiny rest masses of the quarks themselves. In this project QCD is imported context, not a result: the manuscripts state explicitly that confinement and hadron mass are external input, and the program has derived no finite obstruction statement for hadron mass yet.
why: QCD explains why ordinary matter has most of its mass and why isolated quarks are never observed. For this project it marks a program boundary: hadron-mass statements are tagged as imported established physics and must never be presented as program results.
example: A proton is built from two up quarks and one down quark whose combined rest masses are only around one percent of the proton's 938 MeV; the remainder is QCD binding and field energy, often summarized as mass without mass.
conventions: Project prose grades every claim: QCD facts carry the [import] originality tag, and the P1 manuscript states outright that the program does not solve QCD or derive confinement. Do not read the program's finite mass identities as QCD derivations.
source_refs: Wilczek 1999 Mass without mass, Physics Today

summary: A discrete-time quantum version of a random walk: each step, a unitary coin rotation mixes an internal two-state degree of freedom and the walker shifts on a lattice conditioned on it; in this project the split-step 1+1 walk is the arena carrying the derived mass coin.
explanation: Picture a marker on a line of squares. Classically you flip a coin each tick and step left or right. In a quantum walk the coin is a two-state quantum system: instead of landing heads or tails it is rotated into a superposition, and the walker shifts left and right in superposition too, with complex amplitudes that can interfere. The whole update is one unitary operator repeated each tick, so probability is exactly conserved with no approximation. A split-step walk breaks each tick into partial shifts with coin rotations in between; tuned correctly, its long-time behavior reproduces the Dirac equation, with the coin angle playing the role of mass. In this project the mass coin is not a free dial: it is derived from the Plucker area of null steps.
why: Quantum walks show how relativistic wave equations can emerge from strictly local, exactly unitary discrete dynamics, making them a natural testbed for discrete-spacetime programs. Here the program's headline dynamical claim is that the 1+1 split-step walk with the derived complex Plucker mass coin is exactly unitary with an exact group law; this is a kernel-checked draft result, not established physics.
example: The 1+1 split-step Dirac walk: shift the right-handed component one site right, apply the mass coin rotation by angle theta, shift the left-handed component one site left. For small theta and long times, wave packets obey the Dirac equation with mass set by theta.
conventions: Strict unitarity of the discrete-time evolution is the locked arena; the split-step ordering of shifts and coin rotations is fixed per construction and stated explicitly in the manuscript. What the project claims as new is the derivation of the mass coin from null-step geometry, not the split-step walk architecture itself, which is standard.
notation: one tick: U = shift . coin . shift (split-step form)
source_refs: Aharonov, Davidovich, Zagury 1993 quantum random walks

summary: Reflection positivity is the Osterwalder-Schrader requirement that pairing any observable with its own time-reflected mirror image gives a nonnegative number; it is the condition that lets a Euclidean statistical theory be rebuilt as a quantum theory with a true Hilbert space.
explanation: Take a system defined on space plus imaginary time, like a statistical ensemble of field configurations. Reflect everything living at positive times through the time-zero plane, as in a mirror. Reflection positivity demands that pairing any positive-time observable with its own mirror image always yields a nonnegative number. Such pairings behave like squared lengths, so after discarding the zero-length directions (a quotient) they define an honest inner product, which seeds the quantum state space. In this project this step is done at finite size and kernel-checked: for a finite reflected block, reflection positivity plus an explicit compatibility condition makes the null-space quotient a real inner-product space, and exact symmetric 2x2 control examples prove that finite reflection positivity and ordinary matrix positive-definiteness imply neither one another.
why: Reflection positivity is the bridge in the Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction from Euclidean field theory back to quantum mechanics, and it is a standing requirement in mass-gap problems. The project isolates the purely algebraic finite step and separates it cleanly from the unproven positivity of any interacting continuum theory.
example: Among 2x2 symmetric matrices read as two-time correlations, there is a matrix that is positive-definite yet fails the reflected pairing, and another that passes the reflected pairing while failing positive-definiteness, so at finite size the two notions are logically independent.
conventions: Time reflection is taken about the time-zero hyperplane in Euclidean signature, and positivity refers to the reflected pairing, not to entrywise or eigenvalue positivity of the correlation matrix. The project result is the algebraic finite Osterwalder-Schrader step only; continuum reflection positivity of an interacting theory is not claimed.
source_refs: Osterwalder-Schrader 1973 Axioms for Euclidean Green's functions

summary: A regulator is an auxiliary finite or smoothed structure, like a lattice or momentum cutoff, that makes a theory's quantities well defined and computable; in this project the tetrahedral null-direction lattice is a gauge-fixed regulator, not the ontology.
explanation: Think of a smooth photograph and a pixelated copy: you can only do arithmetic on finitely many pixels, but the pixels are a computational stand-in, not the picture itself. A regulator plays that role for a physical theory: an auxiliary finite or smoothed structure, such as a spacetime lattice or a cap on momentum, introduced so that otherwise infinite or ill-defined quantities become finite and computable. Answers about physics should survive when the regulator is refined or removed, and symmetries the regulator breaks must be recovered in that limit. In this project the tetrahedral null-direction lattice is explicitly labeled a gauge-fixed regulator: results proved on it are regulator-level statements, and exact Lorentz-invariance claims for such finite lattices are withdrawn pending a dedicated gate (L0).
why: Without a regulator most quantum field theory computations are ill defined, and which symmetries the regulator preserves controls what must be re-proved in the continuum limit. In this project the regulator-versus-ontology distinction is a locked claim boundary (Gate L0): lattice results stand as mathematics, but covariance claims belong to the ensemble level.
example: Lattice QCD replaces continuous spacetime with a grid of spacing a; quantities are computed on the grid and then extrapolated as a goes to 0. The Wilson term is a regulator artifact: it removes doubler modes at finite spacing and is designed to disappear in the continuum limit.
conventions: Gate L0 (docs/CONVENTIONS.md) locks the claim boundary: the tetrahedral/finite-valency null-direction lattice is a gauge-fixed regulator, not the program ontology; exact Lorentz-invariance claims for finite-valency null graphs are withdrawn, and only ensemble-level statements are covariant.

summary: The renormalization group is the framework for tracking how a system's effective description changes as fine details are averaged out and it is viewed at coarser scales; the couplings that grow, shrink, or hold steady under this flow decide the long-distance physics.
explanation: Zoom out on a photo and pixels blur into shapes; zoom out on a physical system and microscopic details merge into a few effective parameters. The renormalization group makes this precise: coarse-grain by combining blocks of variables into one, then ask what effective interactions the surviving variables feel. Repeating the step generates a flow through the space of possible theories. In this project exactly one such step is a kernel-checked finite identity: blocking lattice sites in pairs and eliminating the fast variables with a Schur complement (a standard block-matrix reduction) provably converts pairwise disagreement between null directions into nonzero effective mass terms, while perfectly aligned (collinear) couplings generate none. It is one decimation step with no limits taken, not a full flow.
why: The renormalization group explains universality, the fact that very different microscopic systems share the same large-scale behavior, and it underlies the modern understanding of quantum field theory. In this project it supplies the mechanism claim that coarse-graining itself manufactures mass from null disagreement, proved in a single exact step.
example: In the block-spin picture of a magnet, replace each 2x2 block of tiny magnets by one majority spin and recompute the effective temperature; iterating the step drives the description toward the ordered, disordered, or critical fixed point.
conventions: The project claim is a single Schur-complement decimation step stated and proved at finite size (RGSchurMassWitness); no continuum limit, fixed point, or full flow is asserted, and program prose must label the result a finite identity rather than an RG theorem about limits.
source_refs: Wilson 1975 renormalization group and critical phenomena

summary: Second quantization upgrades the quantum mechanics of one particle to a framework for any number of identical particles, replacing single-particle states with operators that create and destroy particles in shared modes.
explanation: First quantization describes one particle by a wavefunction. Second quantization changes the bookkeeping: instead of following each particle, track how many particles occupy each available mode, like recording which hotel rooms are occupied rather than tailing one guest. Creation and annihilation operators raise and lower these occupation numbers; for fermions each room holds at most one guest and swapping two guests flips a sign, rules encoded by the canonical anticommutation relations. In this project the lift is finite and kernel-checked: the determinant-minor map Gamma(U) promotes a one-particle walk matrix U to a many-fermion operator whose matrix elements are minors (subdeterminants) of U, and it provably preserves particle number and parity, respects products via Gamma(U V) = Gamma(U) Gamma(V), and sends adjoints to adjoints and unitaries to unitaries.
why: Second quantization is the working language of quantum field theory and many-body physics. In this project Gamma(U) is the exact bridge from the one-particle null-edge walk to many-fermion dynamics, and a kernel-checked no-go shows the interacting pair kick is not Gamma(U) for any one-particle matrix, so genuine interaction lives strictly beyond the one-particle lift.
example: For a two-mode system, Gamma(U) fixes the vacuum, acts on the one-particle states exactly as the matrix U, and multiplies the doubly occupied state by det U.
conventions: Fermionic signs depend on a fixed linear ordering of the modes: matrix elements of Gamma(U) between occupation sets are minors of U with rows and columns taken in that order. The project's finite CAR development fixes the mode order on the finite chain explicitly.

summary: The distance from zero (or from the lowest level) to the rest of an operator's spectrum; a positive gap means no arbitrarily small excitations exist. In this project the phrase is reserved for operator, Hessian, Hamiltonian, mass-matrix, and Dirac-square contexts.
explanation: An operator's spectrum is the set of its possible measured values; for a Hamiltonian these are the allowed energies, and you can picture them as rungs of a ladder. The spectral gap is the empty space between a distinguished rung, often zero or the ground level, and the next rung up. If the gap is positive, the system cannot be excited by arbitrarily gentle pokes: any excitation costs at least the gap. If the gap closes, states exist at every tiny energy and the long-distance, low-energy behavior changes qualitatively. For Dirac-type operators, a gap around zero means no massless modes; a zero mode is precisely a state sitting where the gap would be. Gap size controls decay rates, correlation lengths, and the stability of phases.
why: Gaps are how discrete dynamics hide unwanted branches: a doubler that is gapped stays off-shell. In this repo the language is deliberately disciplined; spectral gap is used only for genuine operator spectra, so the P1 Plucker mass, a finite kinematic invariant, is never oversold as a Hamiltonian gap statement.
example: For a Dirac operator D with mass m, the square D^2 has spectrum starting at m^2: the spectral gap of D around zero is m. In the massless case the gap is zero and zero modes become possible.
conventions: Locked language convention (docs/CONVENTIONS.md): do not use spectral gap as a universal mass slogan. Use it only for operator spectra, Hessians, Hamiltonians, mass matrices, or Dirac-square contexts; for the P1 Plucker mass say finite invariant mass, rank-one obstruction, quadratic Plucker obstruction, or rest-frame invariant of a null bundle.
notation: gap(A) = inf { |lambda| : lambda in spec(A) } (gap around zero)

summary: A spinor is an object whose components transform under rotations in a half-angle way, so a full 360 degree turn multiplies it by -1; spinor fields describe electrons and quarks and are what the Dirac operator acts on.
explanation: A spinor is a column of complex numbers that rotations act on in a half-angle way. Hold a plate flat on your palm and rotate it a full 360 degrees: your arm ends up twisted, and only after 720 degrees is everything back to normal. Spinors track that extra twist: a 360 degree rotation multiplies a spinor by -1, and only 720 degrees returns it to itself. Vectors do not do this; spinors are genuinely different objects, built from the Clifford algebra of spacetime. Electrons and quarks are described by spinor fields, and the Dirac operator acts on them. In this project, finite null spinors psi also build the rank-one matrices P = psi psi^dagger whose determinant carries the mass identity.
why: Every matter particle in the Standard Model is a spinor field, so any program that rebuilds fermions must first get spinors right. In this project the Gate C chirality work asks for kernel and spinor-line projections and richer spin probe representations on the finite substrate.
example: Rotate the two-component spinor (1, 0) about the z-axis by angle theta: it becomes exp(-i theta/2) (1, 0). At theta = 2 pi the spinor has picked up a factor of -1, and only at theta = 4 pi does it return exactly to itself.
conventions: Chirality and handedness labels on spinors are convention choices and must be documented per source (AGENTS.md physics conventions). This project uses the mostly-minus signature and keeps the spacetime chirality grading Gamma_s strictly separate from the internal finite grading chi_E when spinors carry both.
source_refs: Penrose and Rindler, Spinors and Space-Time

summary: A frame of four vector fields, one timelike and three spacelike, attached at each point of spacetime, converting abstract geometry into concrete components; in this project decorations must supply it, because a bare graph does not canonically provide a tetrad.
explanation: General relativity describes spacetime without preferred coordinates, but calculations and spinors need a concrete reference at each point. A tetrad is that reference: four vectors e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3 carried at every point, like a surveyor walking the terrain with one clock direction and three perpendicular rulers. Components of any tensor measured against the tetrad become ordinary numbers, and spinor fields can only be defined once a tetrad, or the equivalent spin frame, exists. In this project's null-edge program the discrete objects are graphs whose edges carry extra data called decorations; the guardrail is that the four-direction frame must come from that decoration data or be derived by an explicit theorem. Claiming a bare graph produces a tetrad conflates causal-order information, which is free, with scale information, which is owed.
why: Tetrads are the bridge between curved geometry and the flat-space spinor algebra where Dirac operators live; without one there are no spinors. In this repo the finite tetrad postulate [nabla_a, C_b] = 0 organizes the Dirac-square decomposition, and the tetrad-provenance guardrail keeps emergence claims honest.
example: In flat spacetime the standard tetrad is e_0 = d/dt, e_1 = d/dx, e_2 = d/dy, e_3 = d/dz. The project's null frame is built from a tetrad by ell_A = e_0 + n_A^i e_i, with dual covectors alpha^A = 1/4 e^0 + 3/4 n_A^i e^i.
conventions: Universal null frames must come from decorated tetrad/spin-frame data unless a separate theorem derives them from the underlying graph (AGENTS.md, docs/NULLSTRAND.md). The Malament split applies: causal order supplies the conformal class for free, and decorations owe exactly the scale. The finite tetrad postulate is [nabla_a, C_b] = 0; failures are classified as nonmetricity, curvature, or related defects rather than hidden.
notation: e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3 (frame); e^0, e^1, e^2, e^3 (coframe)

summary: A repackaging of relativistic kinematics in which light rays, not spacetime points, are the basic objects: a null momentum is encoded by two-component spinors; this project's trusted layer matches its Plucker mass formula in twistor variables with fixed normalizations.
explanation: Ordinary kinematics starts from points in spacetime and four-component momenta. Twistor theory, due to Penrose, flips the picture: the basic object is a light ray, and a twistor is the small package of spinor data that describes one - a two-component spinor giving the ray's null direction, paired with a second spinor recording where the ray passes. A null momentum factorizes into spinor pieces, so questions about collections of light rays become linear-algebra questions about pairs of spinors. That is exactly the shape of this project's mass result: the invariant mass of a bundle of null momenta equals a sum of squared two-by-two determinants, the Plucker areas, of their spinors, and the trusted Lean layer proves the same identity holds when everything is rewritten in twistor variables.
why: Twistor variables make masslessness and chirality structurally transparent and power modern scattering-amplitude methods. For this repo they serve as an independent chart check: the trusted theorem multi_twistor_momentum_det_eq_pairwiseMass confirms the Plucker mass identity is chart-stable rather than an artifact of one parametrization.
example: A single null momentum p with p^2 = 0 factorizes as the rank-one matrix psi psi^dagger for a two-component spinor psi; in twistor language psi is the momentum-spinor part of the twistor describing the corresponding light ray.
conventions: Normalizations between the momentum chart and the twistor chart are fixed explicitly in the trusted layer so the mass identity matches with no drifting factors (NULL_EDGE_RESULTS.md; PhysicsSM/Spinor/TwistorPluckerMass.lean). Mostly-minus signature and the soldering p_0 I + p . sigma are assumed throughout.
source_refs: Penrose 1967 twistor algebra

summary: Weak isospin is the SU(2) charge of the weak interaction; its third component T_3 distinguishes the two members of a left-handed doublet and combines with hypercharge to give electric charge Q = T_3 + Y/2, with generators T_i = sigma_i/2 in this project.
explanation: Left-handed matter particles come in pairs, called doublets: the electron with its neutrino, the up quark with the down quark. Weak isospin is the SU(2) charge that labels this pairing, and its third component T_3 says which slot of the pair a particle occupies: +1/2 for the upper member, -1/2 for the lower. The W bosons of the weak force act like ladder operators that hop a particle between the two slots. Right-handed particles sit alone (singlets) with T_3 = 0, which is why the weak force treats left and right so differently. Electric charge mixes this label with hypercharge: Q = T_3 + Y/2. The generators are built from the Pauli matrices as T_i = sigma_i/2.
why: Weak isospin determines which particles couple to the W bosons and, together with hypercharge, reproduces every electric charge in the Standard Model. In this project, deriving the T_3 assignment and the W ladder structure from octonion ladder operators is the identified S2b gap of the electroweak derivation program.
example: The left-handed up quark has T_3 = +1/2 and Y = 1/3, so Q = 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3; its partner the left-handed down quark has T_3 = -1/2, so Q = -1/2 + 1/6 = -1/3.
conventions: Locked: physics-Hermitian generators T_i = sigma_i/2, Y(H) = 1, Q = T_3 + Y/2, and Higgs vacuum H_0 = (0, v/sqrt(2)). The compact mathematical Lie algebra convention uses anti-Hermitian generators; any theorem stated that way must include an explicit conversion, and factors of i must not migrate silently between generator, connection, and covariant derivative.

summary: A fermion described by a two-component spinor of a single fixed handedness; massless on its own, it gains mass only by pairing with the opposite handedness. Gate C in this project seeks a physical sector with exactly one Weyl line and no doublers returning on-shell.
explanation: Fermions like the electron come in two mirror varieties, left-handed and right-handed. A Weyl fermion is the extreme case: a particle that exists in only one of the two mirror forms, described by just two complex components instead of the four of a full Dirac fermion. Because a standard mass term must couple left to right, a lone Weyl fermion is massless. Neutrinos in the Standard Model are, to good approximation, left-handed Weyl fermions. Discretizing space makes single-handedness notoriously hard: naive lattices always generate extra mirror partners, the doublers, restoring the balance. This project's Gate C is exactly that challenge in the null-edge setting - certify a physical sector containing one Weyl line while every mirror or unwanted branch stays gapped, without off-shell doublers sneaking back on-shell.
why: The Standard Model is chiral - its left-handed and right-handed fermions carry different charges - so any discrete origin story must produce unpaired Weyl fermions, which is precisely what no-go results like Nielsen-Ninomiya obstruct. Gate C is this program's named confrontation with that obstruction, and its guardrails treat branch topology, not coefficient tweaks, as the real problem.
example: Take the dispersion E = +p for a right-mover only: one propagation branch, no partner. A naive lattice version deforms this to a sine curve and adds a second zero crossing at the Brillouin-zone edge - the doubler that restores the mirror partner.
conventions: Chirality and handedness conventions must be documented per source (AGENTS.md). The project keeps spacetime chirality Gamma_s separate from the internal finite grading chi_E. A Gate C claim is release data, not a bare corrected symbol: it needs a selected one-Weyl-line origin sector, true gaps on mirror branches, locality, and anomaly/ghost audits (docs/NULLSTRAND.md). All Gate C results are draft program claims, not established physics.
source_refs: Nielsen-Ninomiya 1981 no-go theorem

summary: A Weyl spinor is a two-component complex vector giving the minimal quantum description of a massless spin-1/2 particle of definite handedness; it encodes a single light-like (null) direction of travel.
explanation: A Weyl spinor is just two complex numbers arranged as a vector psi, yet it captures a massless fermion whose spin is locked to its direction of motion, its handedness or chirality. From psi one can build a light-like 4-momentum, and conversely a light-like direction determines psi up to an overall complex scale, so a Weyl spinor is essentially a square root of a null direction. Massive fermions like the electron need two Weyl spinors of opposite handedness glued together. In this project every null edge carries one visible Weyl spinor, and for a finite bundle of edges the kernel-checked Pluecker mass identity expresses the bundle's invariant mass squared as a determinant built from the pairwise disagreements between those spinors.
why: Weyl spinors are the elementary building blocks of the Standard Model, where every known fermion enters as a chiral two-component field. In this project they are the primitive carriers of the null-edge program: mass is not attached to any single spinor but emerges from how a bundle's spinors fail to align.
example: psi = (1, 0) describes a massless particle moving along the +z axis; bundling it with the non-collinear spinor (0, 1), which points along -z, gives a two-edge system whose total momentum has nonzero invariant mass.
conventions: P1 manuscript conventions: metric signature (+,-,-,-); visible Weyl spinors are complex two-component vectors psi : Fin 2 -> C; the associated null momentum is built from psi and its conjugate. Handedness labels must be stated explicitly whenever both chiralities are in play.

summary: A Wilson term is a momentum-dependent mass added to a lattice fermion operator so unwanted doubler copies become heavy while the intended low-momentum particle stays light; in this project the scalar Wilson route to fixing chirality is proved a sharp no-go.
explanation: Putting fermions on a lattice creates a famous problem: the discretized equation describes not one particle but several identical copies, called doublers, hiding at the corners of momentum space. Wilson's cure is to add an extra term that acts like a mass depending on momentum: it vanishes for the intended particle at zero momentum but grows large at the corners, so the doublers become too heavy to matter. Picture lifting every corner of a trampoline while leaving the center on the floor. The price is that the term breaks chiral symmetry. In this project a sharp no-go is kernel-proved: a purely scalar Wilson-type term can gap the unwanted branches (species health) but provably cannot polarize the balanced zero-momentum kernel into a single chirality.
why: Wilson's term made lattice QCD workable, and its tension with chiral symmetry drove decades of theory (the Ginsparg-Wilson relation, overlap fermions). In this project the scalar Wilson no-go cleanly splits the doubling problem into a plausibly solvable species-health gate (C0) and a genuinely open chiral-release gate (C1).
example: On the momentum torus the Wilson weight W(q) = sum_a (1 - cos q_a) vanishes only at q = 0, so adding r W(q) times the identity leaves the origin mode untouched while giving every doubler corner a mass of order r.
conventions: The Wilson weight satisfies W(q) >= 0 with equality only at the origin, and the coefficient r is positive. The project no-go (C88) is stated for terms that are scalar on the origin corner and vanish quadratically there. A hard ghost rule applies to any release: no gauge-charged branch may be removed solely by a propagator zero; removal must come from a true inverse-propagator mass gap.
notation: r W(q), with W(q) = sum_a (1 - cos q_a)

summary: A Yukawa coupling sets how strongly a fermion interacts with the Higgs field, and after the Higgs takes its vacuum value it becomes that fermion's mass; in this project the Yukawa block B_Y = M : E_R -> E_L is a reconstruction, predictive only if M is constrained.
explanation: In the Standard Model, fermions like electrons and quarks are not born with mass; they acquire it by interacting with the Higgs field. A Yukawa coupling is the number that sets how strongly a given fermion feels that field, a bit like how sticky each particle is in the Higgs medium. When the Higgs settles to its constant vacuum value, each coupling times that value becomes a mass. Left-handed and right-handed parts of a fermion live in different spaces, and the coupling data form a matrix M linking them; the observed masses are the sizes (singular values) of M. In this project the block B_Y = M : E_R -> E_L is labeled a reconstruction: it repackages Standard Model input and predicts nothing unless the architecture constrains M.
why: Yukawa couplings are where all charged fermion masses and the CKM mixing pattern enter the Standard Model, yet their values are unexplained inputs. The project's mass program aims to constrain M from null-edge architecture, and its claim calculus exists precisely to keep that goal from being overstated.
example: The top quark's Yukawa coupling is close to 1, giving a mass near 173 GeV, while the electron's is about 3 x 10^-6; the Standard Model offers no explanation for this hierarchy, which is why an unconstrained M has no predictive power.
conventions: Project claim-status convention (docs/CONVENTIONS.md): B_Y = M : E_R -> E_L is a reconstruction once the Yukawa block is supplied and is predictive only if M is constrained; do not present it as a derivation of fermion masses. The Higgs/Yukawa insertion is tagged as Standard-Model import in the program's claim calculus.
notation: y_f; project block B_Y = M : E_R -> E_L
source_refs: Yukawa 1935 On the Interaction of Elementary Particles

summary: A state an operator sends exactly to zero - an eigenvector with eigenvalue zero; for Dirac-type operators it is an exactly massless state, and in this project a nonzero chiral index forces one to exist no matter how the dynamics are chosen.
explanation: Most states respond when an operator acts on them; a zero mode is a state the operator annihilates outright - output exactly zero, not merely small. For a Dirac-type operator, whose eigenvalues play the role of masses, a zero mode is a perfectly massless excitation. Zero modes are often protected by counting rather than fine-tuning: if left-handed and right-handed states are counted with opposite signs, the total, called the chiral index, is an integer that smooth changes of the dynamics cannot alter. Whenever that integer is nonzero, the books cannot balance without at least one state at exactly zero, so a zero mode survives every deformation. In this project that vanishing-theorem logic is machine-checked at the free level: an invertible overlap operator forces index zero, so nonzero index forces an exact zero mode.
why: Zero modes are how topology talks to spectra: index theorems convert a global integer into guaranteed massless states, underpinning anomalies, edge modes, and topological protection of masslessness. In this repo Gate C2 proves both directions at the free level - a gap forces index zero, and a nonzero index forces a zero mode - including an explicit pi-flux witness.
example: The project's flux witness: a lattice overlap operator threaded with pi flux has nonzero chiral index, so the kernel-checked lemma flux_witness_has_zero_mode exhibits an exact zero mode that persists for every admissible choice of dynamics.
conventions: Zero mode means eigenvalue exactly zero, never approximately small. The chiral index counts zero modes of the two handednesses with opposite signs, so its overall sign follows the chirality convention in use; document that convention when quoting an index value.
source_refs: Atiyah-Singer index theorem
